Reference: Barwick et al. (2025)

Model Setting

The paper asks how much of the decline of more than 90 percent in electric vehicle (EV) battery costs over the past decade is due to learning by doing (LBD), and how LBD interacts with consumer EV subsidies and local content requirements. Two obstacles stand in the way. Battery costs at the vehicle-model level are proprietary and unobserved, and a supplier's cumulative production is endogenous to its cost shocks. The paper solves the first problem with a structural model of the vertical chain: a random-coefficient discrete choice model of EV demand, Bertrand-Nash pricing by EV producers, and Nash-in-Nash bargaining over battery prices between battery suppliers and EV producers. Observed EV prices minus the model-implied downstream and upstream markups give costs, so LBD is estimated without any cost or input data. It solves the second problem with an instrument for experience built from demand shifters (subsidies, rival attributes, the initial supply network and China's whitelist). The data cover annual EV sales, prices, attributes and central-government purchase incentives by model in 13 countries from 2013 to 2020 (over 95 percent of global EV sales, 4,556 model-country-year observations), together with the identity of the battery supplier of every model. Six suppliers dominate (BYD and CATL in China, Panasonic and AESC in Japan, LG and Samsung in South Korea), only 4.3 percent of EV models ever switch supplier, and the vertically integrated BYD and AESC account for 14.5 percent of sales.

The estimated learning rate is 9.2 percent: doubling a supplier's cumulative production lowers the cost per kWh by 9.2 percent, after controlling for industry-wide technological progress, economies of scale, input costs, battery chemistry and experience in EV assembly. LBD explains 42.0 percent of the decline in battery prices between 2014 and 2020 and technological progress another 33.9 percent. Battery suppliers capture only a quarter to a third of the surplus created by their own learning, so learning is under-provided and subsidies raise welfare. LBD and subsidies are strong complements, subsidies in one country spill over to others through shared battery suppliers, and China's whitelist raised domestic welfare at the expense of other countries, but would have lowered it if introduced five years later.

Price Decomposition

EV producer vvv sells the set of vehicles Ωv\Omega_vΩv​, battery supplier bbb supplies batteries for the set Ωb\Omega_bΩb​, and consumer iii considers vehicle model jjj in country ccc and year ttt. The retail price before subsidies pjctp_{jct}pjct​ is decomposed as:

pjct=mcjctb+mcjctv+mkjctb+mkjctv(1)p_{jct}=mc^b_{jct}+mc^v_{jct}+mk^b_{jct}+mk^v_{jct} \tag{1}pjct​=mcjctb​+mcjctv​+mkjctb​+mkjctv​(1)

where mcjctbmc^b_{jct}mcjctb​ is the battery cost, mcjctvmc^v_{jct}mcjctv​ is the non-battery cost of the vehicle, mkjctbmk^b_{jct}mkjctb​ is the battery supplier's markup and mkjctvmk^v_{jct}mkjctv​ is the EV producer's markup. The battery price paid by the EV producer is τjct=mcjctb+mkjctb\tau_{jct}=mc^b_{jct}+mk^b_{jct}τjct​=mcjctb​+mkjctb​. The strategy is to compute the two markups from models of price setting, subtract them from prices, and project the remaining cost on supplier experience.

EV Demand

Demand follows Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995). In each year, consumer iii in country ccc chooses among the available EV models and an outside option, with utility from vehicle jjj:

Uijct=αi(pjct−ϕjct)+Xjctβi+ξjct+εijct(2)U_{ijct}=\alpha_i\left(p_{jct}-\phi_{jct}\right)+\mathbf{X}_{jct}\boldsymbol{\beta}_i+\xi_{jct}+\varepsilon_{ijct} \tag{2}Uijct​=αi​(pjct​−ϕjct​)+Xjct​βi​+ξjct​+εijct​(2)

where ϕjct\phi_{jct}ϕjct​ is the consumer subsidy, so that consumers pay the post-subsidy price. The vector Xjct\mathbf{X}_{jct}Xjct​ contains vehicle size, driving range, horsepower, a plug-in hybrid (PHEV) dummy, a home-product dummy (the automaker is headquartered in the consumer's country, as in Goldberg and Verboven 2001), and market (country-by-year), brand and body-type fixed effects. The term ξjct\xi_{jct}ξjct​ is unobserved product quality, which makes prices endogenous, and εijct\varepsilon_{ijct}εijct​ is an i.i.d. Type-I extreme value shock. The price coefficient depends on income:

αi=α1+αc(i)yi+σpνip(3)\alpha_i=\alpha_1+\frac{\alpha_{c(i)}}{y_i}+\sigma_p\nu^p_i \tag{3}αi​=α1​+yi​αc(i)​​+σp​νip​(3)

where yiy_iyi​ is the income of consumer iii, the coefficient αc(i)\alpha_{c(i)}αc(i)​ varies across four groups of countries ordered by income per capita (China alone forms the first group), σp\sigma_pσp​ is the dispersion of price sensitivity among consumers with similar income, and νip\nu^p_iνip​ is a standard log-normal draw. A negative αc(i)\alpha_{c(i)}αc(i)​ means that low-income households are more price sensitive. Income in each country-year is log-normal with parameters μct\mu_{ct}μct​ and σct\sigma_{ct}σct​ fitted to average income and the income shares of the top 10 percent and the bottom 50 percent from the World Inequality Database. Subsidies enter demand only through the post-subsidy price, which is what later makes them a demand shifter for battery production.

Downstream Pricing

Suppressing country and time indices, EV producer vvv sets the prices of its vehicles in a country-year in Bertrand-Nash competition to maximize variable profit:

πv(p)=∑j∈Ωv(pj−τj−mcjv)qj(p,ϕ)(4)\pi^v(\mathbf{p})=\sum_{j\in\Omega_v}\left(p_j-\tau_j-mc^v_j\right)q_j(\mathbf{p},\phi) \tag{4}πv(p)=j∈Ωv​∑​(pj​−τj​−mcjv​)qj​(p,ϕ)(4)

where τj\tau_jτj​ is the battery price for vehicle jjj, mcjvmc^v_jmcjv​ is the marginal cost of non-battery components, qjq_jqj​ is unit sales and p\mathbf{p}p is the vector of all EV prices in the market. The first-order condition for pjp_jpj​ is:

qj+∑k∈Ωv(pk−τk−mckv)∂qk∂pj=0(5)q_j+\sum_{k\in\Omega_v}\left(p_k-\tau_k-mc^v_k\right)\frac{\partial q_k}{\partial p_j}=0 \tag{5}qj​+k∈Ωv​∑​(pk​−τk​−mckv​)∂pj​∂qk​​=0(5)

The derivatives ∂qk/∂pj\partial q_k/\partial p_j∂qk​/∂pj​ are known once demand is estimated, so inverting this system gives the vector of downstream markups mkv\mathbf{mk}^vmkv with elements mkkv=pk−τk−mckvmk^v_k=p_k-\tau_k-mc^v_kmkkv​=pk​−τk​−mckv​. Joint ventures in China are treated as automakers separate from their local partners.

Upstream: Nash-in-Nash Bargaining

Both layers of the chain are concentrated (a bilateral oligopoly), which motivates bargaining as the preferred model. Contracts are short-term (annual) with linear prices, consistent with publicly released battery supply agreements. Each pair {v,b}\{v,b\}{v,b} chooses the battery price of vehicle j∈Ωv∩Ωbj\in\Omega_v\cap\Omega_bj∈Ωv​∩Ωb​ to maximize the Nash product of the gains from trade, taking the battery prices of all other vehicles as given (Horn and Wolinsky 1988):

NPj(τj,τ−j)=(πv−dv)(1−λb)(πb−db)λb(6)NP_j(\tau_j,\tau_{-j})=\left(\pi^v-d^v\right)^{(1-\lambda^b)}\left(\pi^b-d^b\right)^{\lambda^b} \tag{6}NPj​(τj​,τ−j​)=(πv−dv)(1−λb)(πb−db)λb(6)

where λb∈(0,1)\lambda^b\in(0,1)λb∈(0,1) is the bargaining weight of the battery supplier, πb(τ)=∑j∈Ωb(τj−mcjb)qj(p,ϕ)\pi^b(\boldsymbol{\tau})=\sum_{j\in\Omega_b}(\tau_j-mc^b_j)q_j(\mathbf{p},\phi)πb(τ)=∑j∈Ωb​​(τj​−mcjb​)qj​(p,ϕ) is the supplier's variable profit with per-unit markup mkjb=τj−mcjbmk^b_j=\tau_j-mc^b_jmkjb​=τj​−mcjb​, and dvd^vdv and dbd^bdb are disagreement payoffs. The first-order condition for τj\tau_jτj​ is:

(1−λb)(πb−db)∂πv∂τj+λb(πv−dv)∂πb∂τj=0(7)\left(1-\lambda^b\right)\left(\pi^b-d^b\right)\frac{\partial\pi^v}{\partial\tau_j}+\lambda^b\left(\pi^v-d^v\right)\frac{\partial\pi^b}{\partial\tau_j}=0 \tag{7}(1−λb)(πb−db)∂τj​∂πv​+λb(πv−dv)∂τj​∂πb​=0(7)

If vvv and bbb disagree, vehicle jjj is not produced and consumers move to other EV models or the outside good. Bargaining is model by model, not over a portfolio: battery cells and packs are customized for each model, and a pair bargains over only 2.3 models per market on average. At λb=0\lambda^b=0λb=0 EV producers make take-it-or-leave-it offers and batteries are sold at cost. The variants below differ in the timing of bargaining and downstream pricing, which changes the disagreement payoffs and the two profit derivatives.

Simultaneous Contracting and Pricing

In the preferred variant (Draganska, Klapper and Villas-Boas 2010; Ho and Lee 2017), battery prices and EV prices are set at the same time, so EV prices stay fixed after a breakdown. This fits the annual adjustment of EV prices and is far simpler to compute. The EV producer's disagreement payoff is:

dv,Simult(p)=∑k∈Ωv,k≠j(pk−τk−mckv)q~k(p,ϕ)(8)d^{v,\text{Simult}}(\mathbf{p})=\sum_{k\in\Omega_v,k\neq j}\left(p_k-\tau_k-mc^v_k\right)\tilde{q}_k(\mathbf{p},\phi) \tag{8}dv,Simult(p)=k∈Ωv​,k=j∑​(pk​−τk​−mckv​)q~​k​(p,ϕ)(8)

where q~k(p,ϕ)\tilde{q}_k(\mathbf{p},\phi)q~​k​(p,ϕ) is the sales of vehicle kkk when vehicle jjj is removed at unchanged prices, and the supplier's payoff db,Simultd^{b,\text{Simult}}db,Simult is analogous. Because a marginal change in τj\tau_jτj​ does not move EV prices, it is a pure transfer of qjq_jqj​ between the two parties, and the first-order condition reduces to a split of the gains from trade:

∂πv∂τj=−qj,∂πb∂τj=qj,πb−db,Simult=λb1−λb(πv−dv,Simult)(9)\frac{\partial\pi^v}{\partial\tau_j}=-q_j,\qquad\frac{\partial\pi^b}{\partial\tau_j}=q_j,\qquad\pi^b-d^{b,\text{Simult}}=\frac{\lambda^b}{1-\lambda^b}\left(\pi^v-d^{v,\text{Simult}}\right) \tag{9}∂τj​∂πv​=−qj​,∂τj​∂πb​=qj​,πb−db,Simult=1−λbλb​(πv−dv,Simult)(9)

The gains from trade are πv−dv,Simult=∑k∈Ωvmkkv[qk−q~k]\pi^v-d^{v,\text{Simult}}=\sum_{k\in\Omega_v}mk^v_k[q_k-\tilde{q}_k]πv−dv,Simult=∑k∈Ωv​​mkkv​[qk​−q~​k​] and πb−db,Simult=∑k∈Ωbmkkb[qk−q~k]\pi^b-d^{b,\text{Simult}}=\sum_{k\in\Omega_b}mk^b_k[q_k-\tilde{q}_k]πb−db,Simult=∑k∈Ωb​​mkkb​[qk​−q~​k​], with q~j=0\tilde{q}_j=0q~​j​=0. Stacking over vehicles gives the upstream markups as a function of the downstream markups:

mkb=λb1−λb[Tb⊗S]−1[Tv⊗S]mkv≡λb1−λbmk‾b(10)\mathbf{mk}^b=\frac{\lambda^b}{1-\lambda^b}\left[\mathbf{T}^b\otimes\mathbf{S}\right]^{-1}\left[\mathbf{T}^v\otimes\mathbf{S}\right]\mathbf{mk}^v\equiv\frac{\lambda^b}{1-\lambda^b}\overline{\mathbf{mk}}^b \tag{10}mkb=1−λbλb​[Tb⊗S]−1[Tv⊗S]mkv≡1−λbλb​mkb(10)

where ⊗\otimes⊗ is element-by-element multiplication, Tv\mathbf{T}^vTv and Tb\mathbf{T}^bTb are ownership matrices (the (k,l)(k,l)(k,l) element equals one if vehicles kkk and lll share the same EV producer, or the same battery supplier), and the (j,k)(j,k)(j,k) element of S\mathbf{S}S is qk−q~kq_k-\tilde{q}_kqk​−q~​k​, the change in sales of product kkk when the pair bargaining over vehicle jjj disagrees. The vector mk‾b\overline{\mathbf{mk}}^bmkb is the battery markup at λb=0.5\lambda^b=0.5λb=0.5. Ownership matrices are data and S\mathbf{S}S follows from estimated demand, so battery markups are recovered up to the single parameter λb\lambda^bλb. Upstream markups are modest when the EV producer has little to lose from a disagreement, for example because consumers easily switch to its other models.

Sequential Contracting and Linear Pricing

Under sequential timing (Crawford and Yurukoglu 2012), battery prices are negotiated first and EV producers then compete in prices. Two things change. First, EV prices are reset after a breakdown, so the disagreement payoff must be computed from a new downstream equilibrium for every pair:

dv,Sequential(p~)=∑k∈Ωv,k≠j(p~k−τk−mckv)q~k(p~,ϕ)(11)d^{v,\text{Sequential}}(\tilde{\mathbf{p}})=\sum_{k\in\Omega_v,k\neq j}\left(\tilde{p}_k-\tau_k-mc^v_k\right)\tilde{q}_k(\tilde{\mathbf{p}},\phi) \tag{11}dv,Sequential(p~​)=k∈Ωv​,k=j∑​(p~​k​−τk​−mckv​)q~​k​(p~​,ϕ)(11)

where p~k\tilde{p}_kp~​k​ and p~\tilde{\mathbf{p}}p~​ are the equilibrium prices when vehicle jjj is not produced. Second, both parties internalize the pass-through of battery prices into EV prices and sales, so the supplier's profit derivative gains a demand term:

∂πb∂τj=∑k∈Ωb(1{k=j}⋅qk+mkkbdqkdτj)(12)\frac{\partial\pi^b}{\partial\tau_j}=\sum_{k\in\Omega_b}\left(\mathbb{1}\{k=j\}\cdot q_k+mk^b_k\frac{dq_k}{d\tau_j}\right) \tag{12}∂τj​∂πb​=k∈Ωb​∑​(1{k=j}⋅qk​+mkkb​dτj​dqk​​)(12)

The profit derivatives are (Tv⊗Δτπv)⋅l(\mathbf{T}^v\otimes\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\pi^v}_{\tau})\cdot l(Tv⊗Δτπv​)⋅l and q+(Tb⊗Δτq)⋅mkb\mathbf{q}+(\mathbf{T}^b\otimes\boldsymbol{\Delta}^q_{\tau})\cdot\mathbf{mk}^bq+(Tb⊗Δτq​)⋅mkb, where Δτπv\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\pi^v}_{\tau}Δτπv​ and Δτq\boldsymbol{\Delta}^q_{\tau}Δτq​ collect the derivatives of downstream profits and of sales with respect to battery prices. The bargaining first-order condition becomes:

(1−λb)[(Tb⊗S~)⋅mkb]⊗[(Tv⊗Δτπv)⋅l]+λb[(Tv⊗Mv)⋅l]⊗[q+(Tb⊗Δτq)⋅mkb]=0(13)\left(1-\lambda^b\right)\left[(\mathbf{T}^b\otimes\tilde{\mathbf{S}})\cdot\mathbf{mk}^b\right]\otimes\left[(\mathbf{T}^v\otimes\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\pi^v}_{\tau})\cdot l\right]+\lambda^b\left[(\mathbf{T}^v\otimes\mathbf{M}^v)\cdot l\right]\otimes\left[\mathbf{q}+(\mathbf{T}^b\otimes\boldsymbol{\Delta}^q_{\tau})\cdot\mathbf{mk}^b\right]=0 \tag{13}(1−λb)[(Tb⊗S~)⋅mkb]⊗[(Tv⊗Δτπv​)⋅l]+λb[(Tv⊗Mv)⋅l]⊗[q+(Tb⊗Δτq​)⋅mkb]=0(13)

and solving for the upstream markups:

mkb=−[(1−λb)λb⋅Xt⋅(Tb⊗S~)+(Tb⊗Δτq)]−1⋅qXt=diag([(Tv⊗Δτπv)⋅l]⊘[(Tv⊗Mv)⋅l])(14)\begin{aligned} \mathbf{mk}^b&=-\left[\frac{(1-\lambda^b)}{\lambda^b}\cdot\mathbf{X}_t\cdot(\mathbf{T}^b\otimes\tilde{\mathbf{S}})+(\mathbf{T}^b\otimes\boldsymbol{\Delta}^q_{\tau})\right]^{-1}\cdot\mathbf{q}\\ \mathbf{X}_t&=\text{diag}\left(\left[(\mathbf{T}^v\otimes\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\pi^v}_{\tau})\cdot l\right]\oslash\left[(\mathbf{T}^v\otimes\mathbf{M}^v)\cdot l\right]\right) \end{aligned} \tag{14}mkbXt​​=−[λb(1−λb)​⋅Xt​⋅(Tb⊗S~)+(Tb⊗Δτq​)]−1⋅q=diag([(Tv⊗Δτπv​)⋅l]⊘[(Tv⊗Mv)⋅l])​(14)

where ⊘\oslash⊘ is element-wise division. The diagonal matrix Xt\mathbf{X}_tXt​ is the derivative of the EV producer's profit with respect to the battery price divided by its gains from trade; its diagonal entries are negative (minus the marginal loss from a higher battery price relative to the gains from trade). Unlike the simultaneous case, λb\lambda^bλb no longer enters as a simple scale factor. Linear pricing (double marginalization, Villas-Boas 2007), in which suppliers post battery prices and EV producers then set EV prices, is the special case λb=1\lambda^b=1λb=1 of the sequential model:

mkb=−(Tb⊗Δτq)−1⋅q(15)\mathbf{mk}^b=-\left(\mathbf{T}^b\otimes\boldsymbol{\Delta}^q_{\tau}\right)^{-1}\cdot\mathbf{q} \tag{15}mkb=−(Tb⊗Δτq​)−1⋅q(15)

which is the standard multi-product markup formula applied to the derived demand for batteries.

Bargaining with Dynamic Considerations

LBD gives a supplier a reason to cut today's price in order to accumulate experience and lower future costs. The static models proxy for this with time and supplier fixed effects. The dynamic variant makes battery suppliers forward-looking while EV producers remain myopic. EV producers choose markups, not prices, so that there is full pass-through of battery prices into EV prices (∂pj/∂τj≠0\partial p_j/\partial\tau_j\neq0∂pj​/∂τj​=0, whereas in the simultaneous model ∂pj/∂τj=0\partial p_j/\partial\tau_j=0∂pj​/∂τj​=0 and a supplier cannot buy experience with a lower price). This maximizes the supplier's dynamic incentive. The Nash product is:

NPt(τjt,τ−jt)=(πtv−dtv)(1−λb)(Vtb−Dtb)λb(16)NP_t(\tau_{jt},\tau_{-jt})=\left(\pi^v_t-d^v_t\right)^{(1-\lambda^b)}\left(V^b_t-D^b_t\right)^{\lambda^b} \tag{16}NPt​(τjt​,τ−jt​)=(πtv​−dtv​)(1−λb)(Vtb​−Dtb​)λb(16)

The supplier's payoff under agreement is the present value of profits:

Vtb=∑k∈Ωtbmkktb⋅qkt(mkktv+mkktb+mckt)+∑s=1∞βs∑k∈Ωt+sbmkkt+sb⋅qkt+s(mkkt+sv+mkkt+sb+mckt+s)(17)V^b_t=\sum_{k\in\Omega^b_t}mk^b_{kt}\cdot q_{kt}\left(mk^v_{kt}+mk^b_{kt}+mc_{kt}\right)+\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\beta^s\sum_{k\in\Omega^b_{t+s}}mk^b_{kt+s}\cdot q_{kt+s}\left(mk^v_{kt+s}+mk^b_{kt+s}+mc_{kt+s}\right) \tag{17}Vtb​=k∈Ωtb​∑​mkktb​⋅qkt​(mkktv​+mkktb​+mckt​)+s=1∑∞​βsk∈Ωt+sb​∑​mkkt+sb​⋅qkt+s​(mkkt+sv​+mkkt+sb​+mckt+s​)(17)

where mc=mcb+mcvmc=mc^b+mc^vmc=mcb+mcv is total marginal cost, sales qqq are evaluated at the final EV price mkv+mkb+mcmk^v+mk^b+mcmkv+mkb+mc, and the discount factor is β=0.95\beta=0.95β=0.95. Disagreement lasts one period, after which negotiations resume (Lee and Fong 2013):

Dtb=∑k∈Ωtbmkktb⋅q~kt(mkktv+mkktb+mckt)+∑s=1∞βs∑k∈Ωt+sbmkkt+sb⋅qkt+s(mkkt+sv+mkkt+sb+mc~kt+s)(18)D^b_t=\sum_{k\in\Omega^b_t}mk^b_{kt}\cdot\tilde{q}_{kt}\left(mk^v_{kt}+mk^b_{kt}+mc_{kt}\right)+\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\beta^s\sum_{k\in\Omega^b_{t+s}}mk^b_{kt+s}\cdot q_{kt+s}\left(mk^v_{kt+s}+mk^b_{kt+s}+\widetilde{mc}_{kt+s}\right) \tag{18}Dtb​=k∈Ωtb​∑​mkktb​⋅q~​kt​(mkktv​+mkktb​+mckt​)+s=1∑∞​βsk∈Ωt+sb​∑​mkkt+sb​⋅qkt+s​(mkkt+sv​+mkkt+sb​+mckt+s​)(18)

where q~kt\tilde{q}_{kt}q~​kt​ is sales when product jjj is withdrawn in period ttt and mc~kt+s\widetilde{mc}_{kt+s}mckt+s​ is the future marginal cost, which is higher because the lost sales are lost experience. Three assumptions keep the problem tractable: (A1) suppliers believe that the current market structure, preferences and market size continue forever, so Ωt+sv=Ωtv\Omega^v_{t+s}=\Omega^v_tΩt+sv​=Ωtv​ and Ωt+sb=Ωtb\Omega^b_{t+s}=\Omega^b_tΩt+sb​=Ωtb​; (A2) suppliers ignore the effect of today's battery price on future markups, ∂mkkt+sv/∂τjt=∂mkkt+sb/∂τjt=0\partial mk^v_{kt+s}/\partial\tau_{jt}=\partial mk^b_{kt+s}/\partial\tau_{jt}=0∂mkkt+sv​/∂τjt​=∂mkkt+sb​/∂τjt​=0; (A3) future markups are expected to stay at current equilibrium levels, mkjt+sv=mkjtv∗mk^v_{jt+s}=mk^{v*}_{jt}mkjt+sv​=mkjtv∗​ and mkjt+sb=mkjtb∗mk^b_{jt+s}=mk^{b*}_{jt}mkjt+sb​=mkjtb∗​. Today's price therefore affects future profits only through future sales volumes. The derivative of the supplier's value is:

∂Vtb∂τjt=qjt+∑k∈Ωtbmkktb⋅∂qkt∂pjt+∑s=1∞βs∑k∈Ωtbmkktb∗⋅∑m∂qkt+s∂pmt+sdmcmt+sdτjt(19)\frac{\partial V^b_t}{\partial\tau_{jt}}=q_{jt}+\sum_{k\in\Omega^b_t}mk^b_{kt}\cdot\frac{\partial q_{kt}}{\partial p_{jt}}+\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\beta^s\sum_{k\in\Omega^b_t}mk^{b*}_{kt}\cdot\sum_m\frac{\partial q_{kt+s}}{\partial p_{mt+s}}\frac{dmc_{mt+s}}{d\tau_{jt}} \tag{19}∂τjt​∂Vtb​​=qjt​+k∈Ωtb​∑​mkktb​⋅∂pjt​∂qkt​​+s=1∑∞​βsk∈Ωtb​∑​mkktb∗​⋅m∑​∂pmt+s​∂qkt+s​​dτjt​dmcmt+s​​(19)

The first two terms are the effect on current profit and the last term is the effect on future profits through LBD: a higher τjt\tau_{jt}τjt​ lowers current sales, hence experience, hence raises future costs mcmt+smc_{mt+s}mcmt+s​ and lowers future sales. The static matrices are replaced by dynamic counterparts with elements:

Sjk+=(qkt−q~kt)+∑s=1∞βs⋅(qkt+s−q~kt+s)Δjkt+=∂qkt∂pjt+∑s=1∞βs∑m∂qkt+s∂pmt+sdmcmt+sdτjt(20)\begin{aligned} S^+_{jk}&=\left(q_{kt}-\tilde{q}_{kt}\right)+\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\beta^s\cdot\left(q_{kt+s}-\tilde{q}_{kt+s}\right)\\ \Delta^+_{jkt}&=\frac{\partial q_{kt}}{\partial p_{jt}}+\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\beta^s\sum_m\frac{\partial q_{kt+s}}{\partial p_{mt+s}}\frac{dmc_{mt+s}}{d\tau_{jt}} \end{aligned} \tag{20}Sjk+​Δjkt+​​=(qkt​−q~​kt​)+s=1∑∞​βs⋅(qkt+s​−q~​kt+s​)=∂pjt​∂qkt​​+s=1∑∞​βsm∑​∂pmt+s​∂qkt+s​​dτjt​dmcmt+s​​​(20)

The paper prints the future term of the first line with the index jjj instead of kkk; this is a typo, since the supplier's dynamic gains from trade equal this matrix times the markup vector only with the index kkk, as written here. The static St\mathbf{S}_tSt​ and the demand-derivative matrix Δt\boldsymbol{\Delta}_tΔt​ keep only the first terms. The upstream markup is:

mktb=−[(1−λb)λb⋅Xt⋅(Ttb⊗St+)+(Ttb⊗Δt+)]−1⋅qtXt:=diag([(Ttv⊗Δt)⋅mktv]⊘[(Ttv⊗St)⋅mktv])(21)\begin{aligned} \mathbf{mk}^b_t&=-\left[\frac{(1-\lambda^b)}{\lambda^b}\cdot\mathbf{X}_t\cdot(\mathbf{T}^b_t\otimes\mathbf{S}^+_t)+(\mathbf{T}^b_t\otimes\boldsymbol{\Delta}^+_t)\right]^{-1}\cdot\mathbf{q}_t\\ \mathbf{X}_t&:=\text{diag}\left(\left[(\mathbf{T}^v_t\otimes\boldsymbol{\Delta}_t)\cdot\mathbf{mk}^v_t\right]\oslash\left[(\mathbf{T}^v_t\otimes\mathbf{S}_t)\cdot\mathbf{mk}^v_t\right]\right) \end{aligned} \tag{21}mktb​Xt​​=−[λb(1−λb)​⋅Xt​⋅(Ttb​⊗St+​)+(Ttb​⊗Δt+​)]−1⋅qt​:=diag([(Ttv​⊗Δt​)⋅mktv​]⊘[(Ttv​⊗St​)⋅mktv​])​(21)

which has the same form as the sequential formula with St+\mathbf{S}^+_tSt+​ and Δt+\boldsymbol{\Delta}^+_tΔt+​ in place of S~\tilde{\mathbf{S}}S~ and Δτq\boldsymbol{\Delta}^q_{\tau}Δτq​. The future terms make the supplier's perceived demand more responsive to today's battery price, so a forward-looking supplier accepts a lower markup today. A richer model in which suppliers also internalize future markups is intractable with many sellers and buyers.

Demand Estimation

Demand is estimated by two-step GMM with aggregate and micro moments, following Conlon and Gortmaker (2023). The aggregate moments are:

E[ξjct∣Xjct,Zjct]=0(22)E\left[\xi_{jct}\mid\mathbf{X}_{jct},\mathbf{Z}_{jct}\right]=0 \tag{22}E[ξjct​∣Xjct​,Zjct​]=0(22)

with nine excluded instruments Zjct\mathbf{Z}_{jct}Zjct​. Six are cost shifters: battery capacity interacted with a dummy for each of the top six battery suppliers. Larger batteries cost more and the cost differs across suppliers, while consumers, conditional on driving range, are assumed not to care about capacity or the identity of the supplier (purchase websites do not disclose the supplier). Three are differentiation instruments of Gandhi and Houde (2019): the absolute difference between a vehicle's own size, horsepower and driving range and the average of rivals in the same car type and market-year. There are 104 micro moments. The first type matches the average income of buyers of specific models (50 models in China for 2016 to 2020 and 33 in the United States for 2018, from household surveys). The second type matches the shares of EV buyers in income brackets in Canada, Germany, Norway, Japan, Sweden and the Netherlands (21 moments). These moments identify how price sensitivity varies with income.

Battery Cost and Learning by Doing

After demand estimation, mkjctvmk^v_{jct}mkjctv​ is known and the battery markup is known up to λb\lambda^bλb. The marginal cost of the battery is battery capacity in kWh, BKbjctBK_{bjct}BKbjct​, times a cost per kWh:

mcjctb=BKbjct(γ0EbtγE+CHbjctγ1+PKbtγ2+η∗t)(23)mc^b_{jct}=BK_{bjct}\left(\gamma_0E_{bt}^{\gamma_E}+CH_{bjct}\gamma_1+PK_{bt}\gamma_2+\eta*t\right) \tag{23}mcjctb​=BKbjct​(γ0​EbtγE​​+CHbjct​γ1​+PKbt​γ2​+η∗t)(23)

The supplier's experience is past cumulative production, measured in units of vehicles that sourced batteries from supplier bbb in any country:

Ebt=∑s<t∑c∑j∈I{Ibcs=1}qjcs(24)E_{bt}=\sum_{s<t}\sum_c\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}\{I_{bcs}=1\}}q_{jcs} \tag{24}Ebt​=s<t∑​c∑​j∈I{Ibcs​=1}∑​qjcs​(24)

where qjcsq_{jcs}qjcs​ is the sales of vehicle jjj in country ccc and year sss, and I{Ibcs=1}\mathcal{I}\{I_{bcs}=1\}I{Ibcs​=1} is the set of models in country ccc and year sss supplied by bbb. Experience is firm-specific (internal learning), global, and does not depreciate. The learning coefficient γE\gamma_EγE​ is the elasticity of the learning component of unit cost with respect to experience, and γ0\gamma_0γ0​ is the baseline cost of a supplier that starts production (Ebt=1E_{bt}=1Ebt​=1). The learning rate, or Spence coefficient, is the percentage fall in cost when experience doubles:

learning rate=1−2γE(25)\text{learning rate}=1-2^{\gamma_E} \tag{25}learning rate=1−2γE​(25)

The other terms guard against confounding learning with other sources of cost decline, a concern raised by Thompson (2001): CHbjctCH_{bjct}CHbjct​ is battery chemistry (NMC, NCA or LFP), PKbtPK_{bt}PKbt​ is the capacity of the supplier's median plant in GWh (it enters in logs) and captures economies of scale, lithium prices interacted with battery capacity capture input costs, and the time trend η∗t\eta*tη∗t captures industry-wide technological progress. Because experience grows over time for every supplier, the trend and the learning term compete for the same aggregate decline, and learning is identified from differences in experience across suppliers and over time. Substituting the markups and costs into the price decomposition gives the estimating equation:

pjct−mkjctv=λb1−λbmk‾jctb+BKbjct(γ0EbtγE+CHbjctγ1+PKbtγ2+η∗t)+xvjctγv+fixed effects+ωjct(26)\begin{aligned} p_{jct}-mk^v_{jct}&=\frac{\lambda^b}{1-\lambda^b}\overline{mk}^b_{jct}+BK_{bjct}\left(\gamma_0E_{bt}^{\gamma_E}+CH_{bjct}\gamma_1+PK_{bt}\gamma_2+\eta*t\right)\\ &\quad+\mathbf{x}_{vjct}\boldsymbol{\gamma}_v+\text{fixed effects}+\omega_{jct} \end{aligned} \tag{26}pjct​−mkjctv​​=1−λbλb​mkjctb​+BKbjct​(γ0​EbtγE​​+CHbjct​γ1​+PKbt​γ2​+η∗t)+xvjct​γv​+fixed effects+ωjct​​(26)

where xvjct\mathbf{x}_{vjct}xvjct​ shifts the non-battery cost (vehicle size, horsepower, the PHEV dummy and the log of the EV producer's own cumulative production, which captures learning in assembly), and the fixed effects are for country, EV maker, battery supplier and year. The residual ωjct\omega_{jct}ωjct​ contains cost shocks to both vehicle and battery production. The levels of battery and vehicle costs are not separately identified, since both are absorbed by fixed effects; what is identified is how the price net of the downstream markup varies with battery capacity times a function of experience. For the other supply models, the first term is replaced by the corresponding markup formula. The equation is estimated by two-step GMM.

Identification and Instruments

Three regressors are endogenous. First, experience EbtE_{bt}Ebt​ is correlated with ωjct\omega_{jct}ωjct​: an efficient supplier has sold more in the past if cost shocks are serially correlated, and low-cost suppliers win more EV models, so the network itself is endogenous. The instrument is predicted experience, in the spirit of Benkard (2000) and Covert and Sweeney (2022):

IVbt=∑s<t∑c∑jPr^jbcs(zjbcs) q^jcs(Xcs,ϕcs)(27)IV_{bt}=\sum_{s<t}\sum_c\sum_j\widehat{Pr}_{jbcs}(\mathbf{z}_{jbcs})\,\hat{q}_{jcs}(\mathbf{X}_{cs},\phi_{cs}) \tag{27}IVbt​=s<t∑​c∑​j∑​Prjbcs​(zjbcs​)q^​jcs​(Xcs​,ϕcs​)(27)

Predicted sales q^jcs\hat{q}_{jcs}q^​jcs​ come from the demand model as a function of subsidies ϕcs\phi_{cs}ϕcs​ and attributes Xcs\mathbf{X}_{cs}Xcs​ of all models in the market only, without using prices. The probability Pr^jbcs\widehat{Pr}_{jbcs}Prjbcs​ that model jjj in country ccc and year sss sources from supplier bbb comes from a logit model of supplier choice in the year a model is first released in a country, with shifters zjbcs\mathbf{z}_{jbcs}zjbcs​: a home bias dummy, a whitelist dummy (a Chinese supplier for an EV sold in China in 2016 to 2019), dummies for vertically integrated pairs, the supplier-automaker network in the initial year, supplier age and initial characteristics, and interactions with EV attributes. The instrument uses three sources of variation: (i) subsidies across countries, models and years, since a supplier whose customers receive larger subsidies gains experience faster (China's notched range-based schedule gives discontinuity-type variation); (ii) the attributes of competing EVs, as in BLP instruments; (iii) the initial network and exposure to the whitelist. The assumptions are that, conditional on controls and fixed effects, each of these is uncorrelated with ωjct\omega_{jct}ωjct​. Second, the EV producer's experience is instrumented with its own predicted experience. Third, the markup term mk‾jctb\overline{mk}^b_{jct}mkjctb​ depends on costs and is instrumented with a predicted markup: EV prices are regressed on attributes, subsidies and fixed effects, and shares and both markups are recomputed at predicted prices. The bargaining weight is identified from exogenous shifts in bargaining leverage; the whitelist, for example, strengthened Chinese suppliers, and the response of EV prices reveals λb\lambda^bλb (no response if λb=0\lambda^b=0λb=0).

Key Estimates

  • Demand: in the full model the income coefficients αc(i)\alpha_{c(i)}αc(i)​ are −0.339-0.339−0.339 (China), −0.216-0.216−0.216, −1.378-1.378−1.378 and −0.750-0.750−0.750 for the four country groups, and σp=0.148\sigma_p=0.148σp​=0.148. The average own-price elasticity is −3.48-3.48−3.48 (standard deviation 1.49). The sales-weighted semi-elasticity for a price cut of 1,000 dollars is 10.2 percent in China and 6.3 to 7.5 percent in the other groups. Consumers value range, size and horsepower and show home bias (0.782).

  • Learning: with only experience and fixed effects, γE=−0.218\gamma_E=-0.218γE​=−0.218, which the paper reports as a learning rate of 16 percent (the formula gives about 14 percent). Adding the time trend lowers it to −0.151-0.151−0.151, and the preferred specification with plant capacity and EV producer experience gives γE=−0.140\gamma_E=-0.140γE​=−0.140 (standard error 0.051), a learning rate of 9.2 percent, with γ0=0.958\gamma_0=0.958γ0​=0.958 thousand dollars per kWh. This is far below the 20 to 28 percent of industry studies on aggregate data.

  • Other cost drivers: the time trend is 28 dollars per kWh per year, 2.9 percent of baseline cost; doubling plant capacity lowers cost by 55 dollars per kWh (coefficient −0.080-0.080−0.080); doubling EV assembly experience lowers vehicle cost by 765 dollars (coefficient −1.104-1.104−1.104), which adds up to 3,380 dollars (5.5 percent) over the sample.

  • Bargaining: λb\lambda^bλb falls from 0.504 to 0.311 (standard error 0.104) once controls are added. A weight of 0.311 implies upstream markups of about 142 dollars per kWh, against 313 at a weight of 0.5; CATL's reported markup averaged 83 dollars per kWh in 2015 to 2020.

  • Decomposition: technological progress explains 33.9 percent of the fall in battery prices from 2014 to 2020, LBD 42.0 percent, and scale, chemistry and input costs the rest. In 2014 the learning component γ0EbtγE\gamma_0E_{bt}^{\gamma_E}γ0​EbtγE​​ was 810 dollars per kWh for the top Chinese suppliers, 680 for the South Korean and 550 for the Japanese; Chinese suppliers caught up with the Korean ones by 2018 and with the Japanese ones by 2020.

Alternative Specifications

The learning coefficient is stable across supply models, because the bargaining assumptions move the level of battery prices while LBD is identified from their slope in experience. With battery capacity interacted with year fixed effects in place of the trend, γE=−0.159\gamma_E=-0.159γE​=−0.159. Controlling for the supplier's cumulative patents (instrumented with exposure to EV industrial policies) gives −0.132-0.132−0.132, so learning on the production floor and innovation are distinct. Portfolio bargaining gives −0.143-0.143−0.143 with a bargaining weight of 0.300. Fixing λb\lambda^bλb between 0 and 0.5 in the simultaneous model gives −0.124-0.124−0.124 to −0.157-0.157−0.157; the sequential model gives −0.124-0.124−0.124 at λb=0\lambda^b=0λb=0 and −0.148-0.148−0.148 under linear pricing (λb=1\lambda^b=1λb=1); the dynamic model gives −0.123-0.123−0.123 at λb=0\lambda^b=0λb=0 and −0.141-0.141−0.141 at λb=1\lambda^b=1λb=1. Dynamics matter little because year fixed effects absorb industry-level incentives, suppliers capture a small share of the gains from learning, and at these learning rates the incentive fades within a few years. For spillovers, effective experience is own experience plus a fraction θ\thetaθ of the experience of rival suppliers in the same country; the estimate is θ=0.034\theta=0.034θ=0.034 (standard error 0.102), so learning is essentially internal. Further checks (brand fixed effects, capacity-by-country fixed effects, an instrument without the whitelist, second-order terms in attributes) give γE\gamma_EγE​ between −0.177-0.177−0.177 and −0.119-0.119−0.119.

Market Failures with LBD

Even when learning is internal, it can be under-provided for two reasons. With market power, part of the gain from lower costs passes to consumers through lower prices, which weakens the incentive to learn (the Arrow effect). In a vertical chain, a supplier with limited bargaining power cannot appropriate the surplus that its learning creates downstream. To measure appropriation, the paper raises CATL's (or Panasonic's) experience in 2013 by 10,000 vehicles and simulates the industry to 2020. Normalizing the supplier's own profit gain to one, the global welfare gain is 3.97 for CATL and 3.04 for Panasonic, so CATL captures 25.2 percent and Panasonic 32.9 percent of the surplus from its own learning. With a bargaining weight of 0.5 the shares would be 41 and 43 percent. China captures essentially all of the gain from CATL's learning because its supply chain is domestic, whereas Japan captures only 32.3 percent of the gain from Panasonic's. The private level of experience is therefore below the social optimum.

Counterfactual Algorithm and Network Formation

Counterfactuals use the preferred specification and are simulated forward. In 2013, given costs, battery prices solve the bargaining first-order conditions and EV prices solve the downstream first-order conditions, which gives equilibrium sales. Sales update each supplier's experience, which lowers battery costs in 2014. When new EV models enter, a battery supplier is drawn from a network formation model, and prices and sales are recomputed with the new costs and network; the process is repeated each year to 2020. Because link formation is stochastic, results are averages over 100 simulations. The network formation model is a conditional logit on 23,495 model-supplier-country-year observations, with a choice set of the top 15 suppliers. The coefficients are 0.471 on the eligible subsidy (the subsidy per EV if the link meets the eligibility rule, which is zero for a non-whitelisted supplier in China in 2016 to 2019), 0.666 on log supplier experience, 2.884 on a lagged supplier-automaker link and 0.501 on a lagged link in the same country. Experience thus feeds back into the network: more experienced suppliers win more models. In the whitelist counterfactuals all EV models re-choose a supplier in the first year of the policy. Without LBD, experience is held at its initial level in the sample.

Counterfactuals

Welfare is consumer surplus plus battery and EV variable profits minus subsidy spending, summed over 2013 to 2020, with profits assigned to the headquarters country.

  • LBD and subsidies: relative to a baseline with neither, subsidies alone raise cumulative global EV sales by 27.9 percent (0.83 million units), LBD alone by 95.4 percent (2.83 million), and both together by 204 percent (6.06 million). The joint effect is 65.5 percent larger than the sum of the two, a feedback loop: subsidies raise sales, sales raise experience, experience lowers costs and prices, and lower prices raise sales again.

  • US subsidies: spending of 14.05 billion dollars generates 19.70 billion in global welfare gains, 49 percent of it in North America, and raises local EV sales by 0.84 million. Japan and South Korea gain 7.31 billion (37 percent), mostly as battery profits, because US EVs use their batteries. China gains 2 percent, and Chinese battery suppliers lose 0.34 billion to rivals that learn faster.

  • European subsidies: spending of 18.44 billion generates 14.17 billion in global gains, of which Europe keeps 21 percent, because of imported EVs and uniform subsidies. Japan and South Korea gain 7.54 billion.

  • Chinese subsidies: spending of 31.93 billion generates 42.62 billion in global gains, 92.5 percent of it at home, since China imports few EVs and sources batteries domestically. Without LBD the global gain falls to 5.86 billion.

  • Whitelist: China's local content requirement of 2016 to 2019 raises the sales of Chinese battery suppliers by 16.5 percent over 2016 to 2020 and lowers those of other suppliers by 16.6 percent. Chinese battery profits rise by 4.36 billion, Chinese consumer surplus falls by 0.24 billion, and Chinese welfare rises by 5.41 billion. Chinese EV producers lose in 2016 and 2017 from the switch to costlier domestic batteries but gain 0.45 billion overall as domestic learning accelerates. Europe, Japan and South Korea, and North America together lose 7.65 billion, so global welfare falls by 2.23 billion. Without LBD the effects shrink to 0.63 billion for China and −0.16-0.16−0.16 billion globally.

  • Timing: a whitelist delayed to 2021 to 2024, when battery costs are already below 200 dollars per kWh and foreign leaders are far ahead, raises Chinese battery profits by only 0.66 billion and lowers Chinese consumer surplus by 3.39 billion and Chinese welfare by 1.29 billion. Losses abroad are smaller (1.96 billion for Japan and South Korea). Protection pays only while the learning curve is steep.

This is an accounting identity that organises the whole paper. The retail price before subsidies pjctp_{jct}pjct​ of vehicle jjj in country ccc and year ttt is split into four pieces measured in the same units (thousand dollars per vehicle): the battery cost mcjctbmc^b_{jct}mcjctb​, the non-battery cost mcjctvmc^v_{jct}mcjctv​, the battery supplier's per-unit markup mkjctbmk^b_{jct}mkjctb​ and the EV producer's per-unit markup mkjctvmk^v_{jct}mkjctv​. Nothing is assumed yet; the identity only says that each layer of the chain sells at cost plus markup. The battery price is τjct=mcjctb+mkjctb\tau_{jct}=mc^b_{jct}+mk^b_{jct}τjct​=mcjctb​+mkjctb​, so the identity can also be read in two steps:

pjct=τjct+mcjctv⏟EV producer’s cost+mkjctv,τjct=mcjctb+mkjctbp_{jct}=\underbrace{\tau_{jct}+mc^v_{jct}}_{\text{EV producer's cost}}+mk^v_{jct},\qquad \tau_{jct}=mc^b_{jct}+mk^b_{jct}pjct​=EV producer’s costτjct​+mcjctv​​​+mkjctv​,τjct​=mcjctb​+mkjctb​

Only the left-hand side is observed. The identity becomes useful because the two markups can be computed from models of price setting: mkjctvmk^v_{jct}mkjctv​ from the downstream first-order condition, equation (5), and mkjctbmk^b_{jct}mkjctb​ from the bargaining formula, equation (10), up to the bargaining weight. What remains, pjct−mkjctv−mkjctbp_{jct}-mk^v_{jct}-mk^b_{jct}pjct​−mkjctv​−mkjctb​, is total marginal cost, which is projected on battery capacity times a function of supplier experience in equation (26). As an illustration, a vehicle priced at 40 with markups of 8 downstream and 3 upstream has a total cost of 29; the split of 29 between battery and non-battery cost is not pinned down by the identity and comes from the functional form in equation (23).

This is the indirect utility of a random-coefficient logit model. Consumer iii in country ccc and year ttt buys one of the available EV models or the outside option, whose mean utility is normalised to zero. The first term is the disutility of the price actually paid: the subsidy ϕjct\phi_{jct}ϕjct​ is subtracted from the retail price pjctp_{jct}pjct​, and the price coefficient αi\alpha_iαi​ (negative for a typical consumer) is specific to the consumer, see equation (3). This is the variable profit of EV producer vvv in one country-year. The sum runs over the vehicles Ωv\Omega_vΩv​ that vvv sells. For each vehicle the margin is the retail price pjp_jpj​ minus the battery price τj\tau_jτj​ paid to the supplier minus the marginal cost of the other components mcjvmc^v_jmcjv​; this margin is the downstream markup mkjv=pj−τj−mcjvmk^v_j=p_j-\tau_j-mc^v_jmkjv​=pj​−τj​−mcjv​ of equation (1). Sales qj(p,ϕ)q_j(\mathbf{p},\phi)qj​(p,ϕ) depend on the prices of all EVs in the market and on subsidies through the demand system of equation (2). Three features are worth noting. The subsidy is paid to consumers, so it does not appear in the margin and affects profit only through qjq_jqj​. The battery price is a linear price per unit, with no fixed fee, so it is a marginal cost for the EV producer; this is why there is double marginalisation and why τj\tau_jτj​ shifts EV prices in the sequential model. Fixed costs are omitted because they do not affect pricing. For a vertically integrated producer such as BYD the battery is transferred at cost and τj=mcjb\tau_j=mc^b_jτj​=mcjb​. The profit function is maximised over prices to give equation (5), and it is one of the two payoffs in the Nash product of equation (6).

This is the objective of one bilateral negotiation. The pair formed by EV producer vvv and battery supplier bbb chooses the battery price τj\tau_jτj​ of one vehicle jjj to maximise the weighted geometric mean of the two parties' gains from trade. The gain of vvv is its profit πv\pi^vπv under agreement minus its disagreement payoff dvd^vdv, the profit it would make if vehicle jjj were not produced; the gain of bbb is πb−db\pi^b-d^bπb−db, defined in the same way. The exponent λb∈(0,1)\lambda^b\in(0,1)λb∈(0,1) is the supplier's bargaining weight. At λb=0\lambda^b=0λb=0 the EV producer makes a take-it-or-leave-it offer and the supplier's gain is driven to zero, so batteries are sold at cost; as λb\lambda^bλb rises the supplier's share rises. The label Nash-in-Nash refers to the conjecture that each pair holds: the battery prices of all other vehicles τ−j\tau_{-j}τ−j​ are taken as given, including those negotiated by the same firms for other models, so the outcome is a Nash equilibrium among Nash bargains. Bargaining is over a linear price and not over a transfer, so the price both divides the surplus and, in the sequential model, changes its size. Maximising gives the first-order condition in equation (7). What dvd^vdv and dbd^bdb are, and how πv\pi^vπv and πb\pi^bπb respond to τj\tau_jτj​, depends on timing: equations (8) to (10) for simultaneous timing, (11) to (15) for sequential timing, and (16) to (21) for a forward-looking supplier, where πb−db\pi^b-d^bπb−db is replaced by a difference of present values.

Take logs of the Nash product in equation (6), which does not change the maximiser as long as both gains from trade are positive:

log⁡NPj=(1−λb)log⁡(πv−dv)+λblog⁡(πb−db)\log NP_j=\left(1-\lambda^b\right)\log\left(\pi^v-d^v\right)+\lambda^b\log\left(\pi^b-d^b\right)logNPj​=(1−λb)log(πv−dv)+λblog(πb−db)

∂log⁡NPj∂τj=1−λbπv−dv∂πv∂τj+λbπb−db∂πb∂τj=0\frac{\partial\log NP_j}{\partial\tau_j}=\frac{1-\lambda^b}{\pi^v-d^v}\frac{\partial\pi^v}{\partial\tau_j}+\frac{\lambda^b}{\pi^b-d^b}\frac{\partial\pi^b}{\partial\tau_j}=0∂τj​∂logNPj​​=πv−dv1−λb​∂τj​∂πv​+πb−dbλb​∂τj​∂πb​=0

Multiply by the positive number (πv−dv)(πb−db)(\pi^v-d^v)(\pi^b-d^b)(πv−dv)(πb−db):

(1−λb)(πb−db)∂πv∂τj+λb(πv−dv)∂πb∂τj=0\left(1-\lambda^b\right)\left(\pi^b-d^b\right)\frac{\partial\pi^v}{\partial\tau_j}+\lambda^b\left(\pi^v-d^v\right)\frac{\partial\pi^b}{\partial\tau_j}=0(1−λb)(πb−db)∂τj​∂πv​+λb(πv−dv)∂τj​∂πb​=0

which is the target. Note the crossing: the supplier's gain multiplies the producer's derivative and the producer's gain multiplies the supplier's derivative. Since ∂πv/∂τj<0\partial\pi^v/\partial\tau_j<0∂πv/∂τj​<0 and both gains are positive, whenever λb<1\lambda^b<1λb<1 the condition requires ∂πb/∂τj>0\partial\pi^b/\partial\tau_j>0∂πb/∂τj​>0: the negotiated price is below the price the supplier would post on its own. At λb=1\lambda^b=1λb=1 the condition is ∂πb/∂τj=0\partial\pi^b/\partial\tau_j=0∂πb/∂τj​=0, and at λb=0\lambda^b=0λb=0 it is πb−db=0\pi^b-d^b=0πb−db=0.

Under sequential timing battery prices are agreed first and EV producers then choose prices knowing which vehicles are on the market. If the negotiation over jjj fails, every producer re-optimises: the remaining prices move from p\mathbf{p}p to a new Bertrand-Nash equilibrium p~\tilde{\mathbf{p}}p~​ of the market without jjj, typically higher because competition is weaker. The disagreement payoff therefore differs from equation (8) in two places: the margins use the new prices p~k\tilde{p}_kp~​k​, and sales q~k(p~,ϕ)\tilde{q}_k(\tilde{\mathbf{p}},\phi)q~​k​(p~​,ϕ) are evaluated at the new price vector. Battery prices τk\tau_kτk​ of the other vehicles are not renegotiated, which is the Nash-in-Nash conjecture, so the supplier's markups in its disagreement payoff are unchanged and only its quantities change. Two remarks on the paper's notation. The main text prints the argument on the left-hand side as p\mathbf{p}p, while the appendix writes p~\tilde{\mathbf{p}}p~​; the latter is the consistent one and is used in the note. The appendix also sums over all k∈Ωvk\in\Omega_vk∈Ωv​ instead of k≠jk\neq jk=j; as in the simultaneous case the two are the same because q~j=0\tilde{q}_j=0q~​j​=0. The cost of this timing is computational: a new price equilibrium has to be solved for every vehicle that could be withdrawn. The payoff enters the matrix Mv\mathbf{M}^vMv of profit changes in equation (13), whose (j,k)(j,k)(j,k) element is:

Mjkv=mkkv qk(p,ϕ)−(p~k−τk−mckv)q~k(p~,ϕ)M^v_{jk}=mk^v_k\,q_k(\mathbf{p},\phi)-\left(\tilde{p}_k-\tau_k-mc^v_k\right)\tilde{q}_k(\tilde{\mathbf{p}},\phi)Mjkv​=mkkv​qk​(p,ϕ)−(p~​k​−τk​−mckv​)q~​k​(p~​,ϕ)

Under sequential timing EV prices are chosen after battery prices, so equilibrium prices are a function p(τ)\mathbf{p}(\boldsymbol{\tau})p(τ) and the supplier's profit is:

πb(τ)=∑k∈Ωb(τk−mckb)qk(p(τ),ϕ)\pi^b(\boldsymbol{\tau})=\sum_{k\in\Omega_b}\left(\tau_k-mc^b_k\right)q_k\left(\mathbf{p}(\boldsymbol{\tau}),\phi\right)πb(τ)=k∈Ωb​∑​(τk​−mckb​)qk​(p(τ),ϕ)

∂πb∂τj=∑k∈Ωb(1{k=j}⋅qk+mkkbdqkdτj)=qj+∑k∈Ωbmkkbdqkdτj\frac{\partial\pi^b}{\partial\tau_j}=\sum_{k\in\Omega_b}\left(\mathbb{1}\{k=j\}\cdot q_k+mk^b_k\frac{dq_k}{d\tau_j}\right)=q_j+\sum_{k\in\Omega_b}mk^b_k\frac{dq_k}{d\tau_j}∂τj​∂πb​=k∈Ωb​∑​(1{k=j}⋅qk​+mkkb​dτj​dqk​​)=qj​+k∈Ωb​∑​mkkb​dτj​dqk​​

The total derivative of sales is the chain rule over all EV prices mmm in the market:

dqkdτj=∑m∂qk∂pmdpmdτj\frac{dq_k}{d\tau_j}=\sum_m\frac{\partial q_k}{\partial p_m}\frac{dp_m}{d\tau_j}dτj​dqk​​=m∑​∂pm​∂qk​​dτj​dpm​​

and the pass-through rates dpm/dτjdp_m/d\tau_jdpm​/dτj​ are obtained by totally differentiating the system of downstream first-order conditions, equation (5), with respect to τj\tau_jτj​. Compared with the simultaneous case in equation (9), where the derivative is just qjq_jqj​, the new second term is negative for k=jk=jk=j (a higher battery price raises pjp_jpj​ and lowers qjq_jqj​) and positive for the supplier's other vehicles. The supplier now faces a downward-sloping derived demand, which restrains the battery price it wants even when it has all the bargaining power.

The starting point is the first-order condition, equation (7), for the negotiation over vehicle jjj; the task is to write its four ingredients as row jjj of vectors. For vehicles supplied by bbb the future own-price terms in Δt+\boldsymbol{\Delta}^+_tΔt+​ are negative, so the supplier's perceived demand is more responsive to today's price; in addition the future terms in St+\mathbf{S}^+_tSt+​ are positive, so the supplier has more to lose from a breakdown, and since Xjj<0X_{jj}<0Xjj​<0 this also makes the matrix in brackets more negative. Both effects lower the current markup. Two remarks on the paper: it says that πtv\pi^v_tπtv​ and dtvd^v_tdtv​ are those of the sequential model, but the formula uses the fixed-price matrix St\mathbf{S}_tSt​ of the simultaneous model; and the formula has the same form as equation (14) but Xt\mathbf{X}_tXt​ is built from different objects.

This is the identifying assumption of the demand model: unobserved quality ξjct\xi_{jct}ξjct​ is mean independent of the observed attributes Xjct\mathbf{X}_{jct}Xjct​, which include market, brand and body-type fixed effects, and of the excluded instruments Zjct\mathbf{Z}_{jct}Zjct​. Price is not in the conditioning set, because firms observe ξjct\xi_{jct}ξjct​ when they set prices, so price and ξjct\xi_{jct}ξjct​ are positively correlated and a regression without instruments would understate price sensitivity. In estimation the conditional restriction is used through unconditional moments. For a guess of the nonlinear parameters θ2=(αc(i),σp)\theta_2=(\alpha_{c(i)},\sigma_p)θ2​=(αc(i)​,σp​), mean utilities δjct\delta_{jct}δjct​ are recovered by inverting observed market shares, ξjct\xi_{jct}ξjct​ is the residual of δjct\delta_{jct}δjct​ on price and attributes, and the estimator sets

as closely as possible, together with the micro moments. The nine instruments have two roles. Battery capacity interacted with the identity of the six largest suppliers shifts cost and hence price; the exclusion restriction is that, conditional on driving range, consumers do not value capacity or the supplier's identity. The three differentiation instruments measure how isolated a vehicle is in attribute space; they shift markups and identify substitution patterns, that is, σp\sigma_pσp​. The assumption that attributes are exogenous is the usual one in this literature and rules out producers choosing range or size in response to ξjct\xi_{jct}ξjct​. The estimated demand system delivers the derivatives and diversion quantities used in equations (5), (10) and (27).

The battery cost of vehicle jjj is its capacity BKbjctBK_{bjct}BKbjct​ in kWh times a cost per kWh, which follows the industry convention of quoting costs per kWh and makes a large pack proportionally more expensive. The cost per kWh, in thousand dollars, has four additive parts. The learning part γ0EbtγE\gamma_0E_{bt}^{\gamma_E}γ0​EbtγE​​ is a power function of the supplier's experience EbtE_{bt}Ebt​ defined in equation (24): γ0\gamma_0γ0​ is the cost at Ebt=1E_{bt}=1Ebt​=1, and γE<0\gamma_E<0γE​<0 is the elasticity of this part with respect to experience,

∂log⁡(γ0EbtγE)∂log⁡Ebt=γE\frac{\partial\log\left(\gamma_0E_{bt}^{\gamma_E}\right)}{\partial\log E_{bt}}=\gamma_E∂logEbt​∂log(γ0​EbtγE​​)​=γE​

so each doubling of experience cuts it by the constant fraction in equation (25), and the absolute gains from learning shrink as experience accumulates. The term CHbjctγ1CH_{bjct}\gamma_1CHbjct​γ1​ shifts cost by chemistry (NMC, NCA, LFP). The term PKbtγ2PK_{bt}\gamma_2PKbt​γ2​ captures economies of scale through the log capacity of the supplier's median plant. The trend η∗t\eta*tη∗t is technological progress common to all suppliers. With the preferred estimates, γ0=0.958\gamma_0=0.958γ0​=0.958 and γE=−0.140\gamma_E=-0.140γE​=−0.140, a supplier with experience of 100,000 vehicles has a learning component of 0.958×100000−0.140≈0.1910.958\times100000^{-0.140}\approx0.1910.958×100000−0.140≈0.191, that is, 191 dollars per kWh. Because the parts are additive, the learning rate applies to the learning part and not to the whole cost per kWh, whose proportional fall is smaller. The additive controls are what prevent γE\gamma_EγE​ from absorbing other sources of cost decline; the price is that learning does not interact with them. The specification enters the estimating equation (26) and drives the forward simulation in the counterfactuals.

Experience of supplier bbb at the start of year ttt is the number of vehicles, summed over all earlier years s<ts<ts<t and all countries ccc, that were sold with a battery from bbb. The inner set I{Ibcs=1}\mathcal{I}\{I_{bcs}=1\}I{Ibcs​=1} collects the models in country ccc and year sss whose supplier is bbb, and qjcsq_{jcs}qjcs​ is their sales. Several modelling choices are built into the definition. Experience is counted in vehicles, not in kWh, so a small and a large pack add the same amount. It is global: sales in any country add to the same stock, which is what creates cross-country spillovers of subsidies through shared suppliers. It is internal: only the supplier's own output counts, and the extension with a spillover parameter θ\thetaθ on rival experience finds a value close to zero. It does not depreciate, so there is no organisational forgetting. It is lagged, since the sum stops at t−1t-1t−1, which implies the recursion

Ebt+1=Ebt+∑c∑j∈I{Ibct=1}qjctE_{bt+1}=E_{bt}+\sum_c\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}\{I_{bct}=1\}}q_{jct}Ebt+1​=Ebt​+c∑​j∈I{Ibct​=1}∑​qjct​

used to simulate the counterfactuals: sales in year ttt lower costs from year t+1t+1t+1 on through equation (23). The lag removes simultaneity between current cost shocks and current sales, but not endogeneity: with serially correlated cost shocks, a supplier with low costs sold more in the past, so EbtE_{bt}Ebt​ is correlated with ωjct\omega_{jct}ωjct​ in equation (26). This is why the instrument in equation (27) replaces actual sales and actual supplier links with predicted ones.

The instrument has the same structure as experience in equation (24), a sum over past years s<ts<ts<t and countries ccc, but replaces the two endogenous ingredients with predictions built from exogenous variables. The instrument is expected cumulative sales:

IVbt=∑s<t∑c∑jE[1{j sources from b}∣zjbcs]⋅E[qjcs∣Xcs,ϕcs]IV_{bt}=\sum_{s<t}\sum_c\sum_jE\left[\mathbb{1}\{j\text{ sources from }b\}\mid\mathbf{z}_{jbcs}\right]\cdot E\left[q_{jcs}\mid\mathbf{X}_{cs},\phi_{cs}\right]IVbt​=s<t∑​c∑​j∑​E[1{j sources from b}∣zjbcs​]⋅E[qjcs​∣Xcs​,ϕcs​]

Relevance holds because subsidies and weak competition raise actual sales and hence actual experience. Exclusion requires that, conditional on the controls and fixed effects of equation (26), subsidies, rival attributes, the initial network and exposure to the whitelist are unrelated to the cost shock ωjct\omega_{jct}ωjct​. A simple illustration: two suppliers with identical technology, one of which serves models that qualify for a larger subsidy; the latter accumulates predicted experience faster, and if its battery prices also fall faster, the difference is attributed to learning. Since the cost function is nonlinear in EbtE_{bt}Ebt​, the instrument enters the GMM moments for equation (26) and is not used in a linear first stage.
